definition: Grotesque means distorted or misshapen to the point of being disturbing — ugly in a warped, unnatural, often darkly comic way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word grotesque. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know grotesque should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The cathedral's stonemasons saved their grotesque inventions for the rain spouts: dog-faced men, grinning imps, a monk with a serpent's tail.
Odd is far milder than grotesque — a detail slightly out of place, met with a shrug rather than a shudder.
Nightmarish goes further than grotesque: the distortion deepens until the sight belongs in a bad dream and follows you out of it.

Hideous is pure ugliness at full strength — a thing so ugly it repels. Grotesque is more particular: the ugliness comes from distortion, natural forms twisted or mismatched, and it can carry a streak of dark comedy that hideous never has.

Monstrous makes a thing a monster — frightening, often enormous, and morally dreadful in extended use. Grotesque stays closer to the eye: it names shapes gone wrong, warped and exaggerated, disturbing more than terrifying.

That double edge is the word's signature — grotesque things are not simply ugly; they are distortions of something we know, and the laughter they raise always has a shiver in it.

Writers extend it to abstractions the same way — a grotesque injustice is one twisted far out of any recognizable shape.

The monastery's account books are dull reading until you reach the margins.
There, some bored twelfth-century clerk let his pen wander: a rabbit with a bishop's head, a snail wearing armor and human feet, a choir of frogs with too many mouths.
Scholars catalogue these drawings as grotesque, and the label is precise.
Each figure takes natural forms and twists them together until the result is wrong in a way the eye cannot settle.
Yet almost no one calls them frightening.
Visitors to the exhibit laugh first and grimace second.
That double response — the snicker riding on the shudder — is what separates the margins from a nightmare.
